conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here.  
I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. Over the next few minutes I’d like to check in with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied set of ten questions that helps us see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything we discuss stays confidential within your care team. My goal is simply to understand what’s been going on for you so we can make sure you have the support you deserve. We’ll go one question at a time, focusing on the past seven days. Ready to start?

To begin: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I... I can laugh sometimes, usually at little things my baby does—like when he makes those funny faces while he’s asleep. But mostly it feels like work to smile, and when other people tell jokes or try to cheer me up, I just feel too tired or worried to really laugh along. It’s like the joy is behind a glass wall—I can see it, but I can’t quite reach it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes… that’s right. I have been able to laugh, but only sometimes, and it takes a lot of effort. Most of the time I have to force it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with my neighbor—but the excitement just isn’t really there anymore. I’ll mark it on the calendar and hope it’ll feel special, yet when the moment comes it feels flat, like I’m just going through the motions.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby spits up a lot, I think it must be something I ate. If he fusses, I assume I’m not soothing him right. When I couldn’t get the laundry folded yesterday, I told myself I’m a lousy wife and a terrible mom. I know, rationally, babies just cry and spit up, but the voice in my head still says it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Almost every day. Even when the baby’s sleeping peacefully, I catch myself staring at the monitor, convinced something will go wrong. My heart races and I can’t settle. I’ll make up these awful scenarios—like him choking or getting sick—and then I’m too tense to sleep or eat. It’s like I’m always bracing for disaster, even when nothing’s actually happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… several times this week. I’ll be folding tiny onesies and suddenly feel like I can’t breathe, like the walls are closing in or I’m about to drop the baby even though he’s safe in the crib. My chest gets tight, my hands shake, and I have to sit down and count my breaths until it passes. It’s scary because it comes out of nowhere, and I worry it means something’s really wrong with me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs feeding, texts go unanswered, and it all feels like too much. I’ll start one chore, hear him cry, rush over, then forget what I was doing, and the cycle repeats. By evening I’m exhausted and convinced I can’t handle even tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down and my mind just keeps spinning—worrying about the baby, replaying everything I did wrong that day, imagining awful “what-ifs.” Even when he’s asleep for three- or four-hour stretches, I can’t drift off. I’ll stare at the ceiling until finally I doze, then jolt awake at every tiny sound. I’m exhausted, but the sadness and worry keep chasing sleep away.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes… pretty much every day this week. I wake up already feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest that won’t lift. I’ll look at my beautiful baby and feel like I *should* be happy, but instead I just feel empty or like I want to cry. Even when I try to tell myself, “This is temporary,” the sadness keeps settling back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried several times this week. Sometimes it’s when the baby won’t settle and I feel useless, or when my partner asks how I’m doing and I just lose it. A couple of nights I’ve laid in bed with tears running down because I feel so overwhelmed and alone, even though people keep saying they’re here for me.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I get really low, but I’ve never pictured ending things or doing anything like that. I just want to feel better for my baby’s sake—and for mine.

You've shared how most days feel heavy and joyless since your baby arrived-laughter comes only with effort, excitement feels flat, and waves of worry or even panic strike without warning. Despite loving your little one, you carry a constant sense of failing as a mom, and tears arrive easily when tasks pile up. Even when your baby sleeps, your mind races through frightening "what-ifs," leaving you exhausted yet unable to rest.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient can laugh only sometimes and with effort, mapping to "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished anticipation and pleasure, indicating "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" for routine infant behaviors, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, catastrophizing worries with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes this week with intense physical symptoms (breathlessness, shaking, chest tightness), classic for "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and anticipatory hopelessness, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-nightly inability to sleep due to racing worries and persistent unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "pretty much every day this week" and describes persistent, heavy sadness that "keeps settling back in," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent crying episodes tied to feeling overwhelmed and alone, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of ≥14 signals probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>; with 25 points, your responses map to the core criteria: <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>diminished interest</sym> most of the day, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>recurrent crying</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and <sym>difficulty coping</sym>. These symptoms, present nearly every day for two weeks, suggest moderate-to-severe symptom load requiring immediate evaluation. You denied self-harm thoughts, so acute safety risk is lower, but impairment is high. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, <med>CBT</med>, or <med>sertraline</med>/<med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Involve trusted family or friends in daily tasks-meals, laundry, night shifts-to create rest periods
4. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic</sym> rises; keep baby nearby in a safe spot if you need to step away briefly
5. Maintain basic self-care: hydrate, eat small frequent meals, and accept that household chores can wait
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress once treatment begins
7. Store 24-h hotline numbers in your phone: <med>Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773</med> and local crisis text line for immediate support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Structured Note

Patient-reported symptoms (≥2 wks):
- Persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, anhedonia (“flat,” “empty”)
- Marked guilt / self-blame re infant care
- Panic-type episodes (dyspnea, tremor, derealization) and near-constant intrusive “what-ifs” about infant safety
- Initial and middle insomnia even when infant sleeps
- Feeling “drowning,” unable to cope with routine tasks

Pattern: symptoms present “most days,” causing distress and functional impairment; no self-harm ideation endorsed.

Screening significance:
- High endorsement on EPDS-equivalent items for depression (mood, loss of enjoyment, self-blame, crying, sleep) and anxiety (worry, panic)
- No current suicidal ideation; safety risk low per patient statement

Next step: recommend comprehensive evaluation with OB/GYN or mental health clinician to rule out major postpartum depressive and/or anxiety disorder and discuss evidence-based treatment options.
